lead: This unit teaches how to convert text into feature vectors and classify documents, sentences or reviews. You will compute TF-IDF, train Naive Bayes, logistic regression and SVM, evaluate with precision and recall, and build sentiment classifiers. You will also learn one-hot vectors, Word2Vec, GloVe, Doc2Vec and document clustering.
about: This unit turns text into numbers a classifier can use, then measures and applies the classifier. Chapter 5.1 builds bag-of-words and TF-IDF vectors. Chapter 5.2 trains Naive Bayes, logistic regression and linear SVM on those vectors. Chapter 5.3 adds feature engineering and evaluation metrics such as precision, recall and F1. Chapter 5.4 applies these ideas to sentiment analysis, both lexicon-based and machine learning. Chapter 5.5 moves from sparse one-hot vectors to dense word vectors. Chapter 5.6 explains Word2Vec, GloVe and Doc2Vec. Chapter 5.7 uses distributional semantics and document clustering to group similar texts. The later chapters depend on the earlier vector and classifier ideas.

chapters.idea: Text becomes a vector of term counts or TF-IDF weights so a classifier can use it.
chapters.depth: Vocabulary building, bag-of-words counts, binary bag-of-words, and n-gram features. TF-IDF: tf(t,d)=count(t,d)/|d|, idf(t)=log(N/df(t)), weight=tf×idf; N is number of documents, df(t) is number of documents containing term t, |d| is number of terms in document d. Cover variants: add-one smoothing, log scaling, sublinear tf, and L2 normalization. Some syllabi call this term weighting or the vector space model.

figure.title: TF-IDF matrix, log10; columns: cricket, bat, ball, stock, market
figure.aria: A three-row matrix shows TF-IDF weights for documents D1 to D3 over five terms.

chapters.example: Three documents: D1 = cricket bat ball; D2 = cricket ball; D3 = stock market. Build the vocabulary and compute TF-IDF with tf = count/|d| and idf = log10(3/df). Give the 3×5 matrix.
chapters.trap: Using raw term counts as TF-IDF, or forgetting that df is counted across all documents; idf changes when new documents are added.
chapters.leave: N-gram language models to Unit 2; cosine similarity details to 5.5.

chapters.idea: Supervised classifiers map text feature vectors to labels by learning weights or probabilities from labelled examples.
chapters.depth: Multinomial Naive Bayes: P(c|d) ∝ P(c)∏P(t|c), with Laplace smoothing P(t|c)=(count(t,c)+1)/(count(c)+|V|). Logistic regression: p(y=1|x)=1/(1+e^(−w·x)); softmax for multiclass; minimize cross-entropy. Linear SVM: maximize margin and minimize hinge loss max(0,1−y(w·x+b)); mention kernel trick. Some syllabi add decision trees; only a few universities examine them.

figure.aria: A left-to-right flow shows training documents, word counts, add-one smoothing, class scores and a positive prediction.

chapters.example: Training data: positive = good film; negative = bad film. Vocabulary = {good, bad, film}. Use add-one Naive Bayes. Test the document good film. Prior P(pos)=P(neg)=1/2. P(good|pos)=2/5, P(film|pos)=2/5, positive score = 0.08. P(good|neg)=1/5, P(film|neg)=2/5, negative score = 0.04. Predict positive.
chapters.trap: Forgetting Laplace smoothing gives zero likelihood for an unseen word; raw probabilities can underflow, so use log scores.
chapters.leave: Neural text classifiers and CNNs to Unit 6; named entity recognition to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Good text features and the right evaluation metric decide whether a classifier is actually useful.
chapters.depth: Feature types: word n-grams, character n-grams, TF-IDF, presence flags, document length, punctuation and POS tags. Feature selection with chi-square and mutual information. Class imbalance. Metrics from the confusion matrix: precision=TP/(TP+FP), recall=TP/(TP+FN), F1=2PR/(P+R), accuracy=(TP+TN)/total; macro and micro averaging; ROC-AUC; cross-validation.

figure.title: Confusion matrix; columns: actual spam, actual ham
figure.aria: A two-by-two confusion matrix shows 80 true spam, 20 false spam, 10 missed spam and 890 true ham.

chapters.example: A spam classifier is tested on 1000 emails: TP=80, FP=20, FN=10, TN=890. Compute precision, recall, F1 and accuracy.
chapters.trap: Accuracy of 97% hides 10 missed spam out of 90 spam emails; report precision and recall on the rare class.
chapters.leave: Detailed model tuning and neural metrics to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Sentiment analysis assigns polarity or emotion to text using either a lexicon or a trained classifier.
chapters.depth: Types: binary, multi-class and aspect-based sentiment. Lexicon-based scoring: word polarity scores, negation, intensifiers and contrast words; mention SentiWordNet-style lexicons. Machine learning approaches: Naive Bayes, logistic regression and SVM on 5.1–5.3 features. Evaluation with precision, recall and F1, including per-aspect evaluation.

figure.aria: A flow shows tokens, lexicon scores, negation handling, total score and aspect-level polarity.

chapters.example: Lexicon: good=+2, excellent=+3, bad=−2; negator not=−1 multiplied by the next word. Sentence: not good but excellent songs. Score not good = −2; excellent = +3; total = +1, so positive. Aspect view: film is negative, songs are positive.
chapters.trap: Ignoring negation treats not good as positive; lexicon polarity also depends on domain, and one overall score can hide opposite aspect polarities.
chapters.leave: Speech emotion recognition to Unit 7; review-specific neural models to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A word can be represented as a sparse one-hot vector or as a dense vector whose geometry encodes similarity.
chapters.depth: One-hot vectors have length |V| and are orthogonal. Cosine similarity: cos(a,b)=(a·b)/(|a||b|). Co-occurrence matrix, positive pointwise mutual information (PPMI), and SVD/LSA for dense vectors. Some syllabi call this vector semantics or distributed representations.

figure.title: One-hot and dense vectors; dense columns: dim1, dim2
figure.aria: Rows show two one-hot vectors and two dense two-number vectors for cricket and bat.

chapters.example: Vocabulary = {cricket, bat, ball}. One-hot: cricket=[1,0,0], bat=[0,1,0]; their cosine is 0. Dense: cricket=[0.8,0.2], bat=[0.6,0.4]. Dot product = 0.56; |cricket|=√0.68≈0.825; |bat|=√0.52≈0.721; cosine≈0.942.
chapters.trap: One-hot vectors are all orthogonal, so cosine cannot show word similarity; dense vectors must be compared with a normalized similarity measure.
chapters.leave: Word2Vec and GloVe to 5.6; contextual BERT vectors to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Word2Vec and GloVe learn dense word vectors from context, and Doc2Vec adds a learned vector for a whole document.
chapters.depth: Word2Vec: CBOW predicts a target from context; skip-gram predicts context from a target; negative sampling and hierarchical softmax. GloVe uses global co-occurrence counts and a weighted least-squares objective. Doc2Vec: PV-DM and PV-DBOW add a document ID to the model. Cover vector analogies and nearest neighbours. Mention FastText subword vectors only briefly; only a few universities teach it.

figure.aria: A two-dimensional graph places man, woman, king and queen as points; the vector step from king to queen is minus man plus woman.

chapters.example: Given man=[1,0], woman=[0,1], king=[1,1], compute king − man + woman. The result is [0,2], which is the vector given for queen.
chapters.trap: Raw dot products are not comparable across vector lengths; use cosine. Analogy arithmetic is approximate and depends on the training corpus and window size.
chapters.prereq: 5.5 one-hot and dense vectors; cosine similarity.
chapters.leave: BERT, GPT, transformers and large language models to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Words and documents that appear in similar contexts get similar vectors, and clustering groups documents by vector similarity.
chapters.depth: Distributional hypothesis: similar contexts give similar meanings. Co-occurrence counts, PPMI, and SVD. Document vectors from TF-IDF or Doc2Vec. Clustering: k-means with cosine or Euclidean distance, assign to nearest centroid, recompute centroids, repeat; hierarchical clustering briefly. Evaluation: purity and silhouette score. Mention topic modelling as a related method without detail.

figure.aria: A two-dimensional graph shows four document points and their two centroids; D1 and D2 form one cluster, D3 and D4 form the other.

chapters.example: Four document vectors: D1=[3,0], D2=[2,1], D3=[0,3], D4=[1,2]. Run k-means with k=2, starting centroids C1=D1 and C2=D3. Show the first assignment and the updated centroids.
chapters.trap: k-means depends on the initial centroids and on k; Euclidean and cosine distance can give different clusters; cluster numbers have no meaning.
chapters.leave: Word sense disambiguation and WordNet to Unit 4; semantic parsing to Unit 4.
